1.pericope_label: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying, Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the Lord thy God said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel. Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the Lord by Samuel.

schools.summary: Delitzsch maps the chapter onto 2 Samuel 5 and 23 and supplies the seven years of civil war the chronicler passes over; Ellicott reads the omission as deliberate, argues from "all Israel" that this is not the Judah-only anointing, and treats the covenant with the elders as a genuine constitutional contract settling the manner of the kingdom.
Clarke declines to expound the passage at all, printing only an outline and referring the reader to his notes on 2 Samuel 5 as already covering the ground.

Henry reads the covenant morally, as the original contract between prince and people which both ought religiously to observe, and argues a fortiori that David, of all men the safest to trust with absolute power, still bound himself to rule by law.

debates: Whether the anointing at Hebron was the act of the king in person or through the elders as his organ, and how much constitutional weight the covenant of verse 3 carries.
Whether Chronicles here is an independent narrative or a duplicate of 2 Samuel needing no separate comment.
outliers: Ellicott supports the divine right implied in "thou shalt feed my people" from the cuneiform documents, where "shepherd" is applied to sovereigns as far back as the pre-Semitic stage of Babylonian civilisation.
themes: Then all Israel gathered themselves to David unto Hebron, saying, Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh.

And moreover in time past, even when Saul was king, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel: and the Lord thy God said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be ruler over my people Israel.

Therefore came all the elders of Israel to the king to Hebron; and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord; and they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the Lord by Samuel.

4.pericope_label: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus; where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, Thou shalt not come hither. Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David. And David said, Whosoever smiteth the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain. So Joab the son of Zeruiah went first up, and was chief. And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David. And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about: and Joab repaired the rest of the city. So David waxed greater and greater: for the Lord of hosts was with him.

schools.summary: Ellicott collates the capture of Jebus against 2 Samuel 5 clause by clause, finding the chronicler following a clearer source than Samuel's obscure but evidently original record, and reads the Millo passage as a complete circuit of defences; Delitzsch notes that the verb used of Joab's rebuilding means to make alive, as at Nehemiah 4:2 of ruins.
Wesley takes Joab's reward as a national promotion, from one of David's chief captains to captain-general of all the forces of Israel and Judah.
Henry ignores the office and asks what produced the exploit, finding the answer in opposition and in the prospect of preferment.

debates: What Joab won at Jebus: Ellicott suggests head and governor of Jerusalem, since Joab was already David's general under Ishbosheth, while Wesley makes it command of all the forces of Israel and Judah.
Whether David's building ran round from the Millo and back to it, as the chronicler seems to say, or from the Millo inward, as Samuel has it.
outliers: Ellicott derives "Lord of hosts" from the host of heaven, noting that in old Babylonian the word for God is written with a star and that Assur is titled king of the legions of heaven and earth.
themes: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus; where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land.
And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, Thou shalt not come hither. Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David.

And David dwelt in the castle; therefore they called it the city of David.
And he built the city round about, even from Millo round about: and Joab repaired the rest of the city.
So David waxed greater and greater: for the Lord of hosts was with him.

10.pericope_label: These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the Lord concerning Israel. And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time. And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighties. He was with David at Pas–dammim, and there the Philistines were gathered together to battle, where was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines. And they set themselves in the midst of that parcel, and delivered it, and slew the Philistines; and the Lord saved them by a great deliverance. Now three of the thirty captains went down to the rock to David, into the cave of Adullam; and the host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim. And David was then in the hold, and the Philistines’ garrison was then at Beth–lehem. And David longed, and said, Oh that one would give me drink of the water of the well of Beth–lehem, that is at the gate! And the three brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Beth–lehem, that was by the gate, and took it, and brought it to David: but David would not drink of it, but poured it out to the Lord, And said, My God forbid it me, that I should do this thing: shall I drink the blood of these men that have put their lives in jeopardy? for with the jeopardy of their lives they brought it. Therefore he would not drink it. These things did these three mightiest.

schools.summary: Ellicott diagnoses a substantial lacuna after "the Philistines were gathered together", restores the lost lines from Samuel, and traces the consequent corruption of Shammah's singular verbs into plurals; Delitzsch defends "the thirty chiefs" against Thenius.

Clarke carries Kennicott's count of about thirty-four Hebrew words lost here and preserved in Samuel, and prints the Targum's expansion of David as anointed judge; Wesley harmonises the three hundred of Chronicles with the eight hundred of Samuel by crediting the surplus to those who joined the pursuit.

Henry takes the register as commentary on the preceding verse, noting that a great man's strength is borrowed from his servants, and finds in the poured-out water four honourable dispositions in David.

debates: Whether Jashobeam slew three hundred, as Chronicles has it, or eight hundred as in Samuel: Ellicott keeps the smaller figure on text-critical grounds while Wesley harmonises the two.
Whether the title means head of the Thirty, head of the knights, or head of the Three.
Whether the pouring out of the water is chiefly a sacrificial act, as Ellicott takes it, or chiefly a moral one, as Henry and Wesley read it.
outliers: Ellicott is unembarrassed by the three hundred, comparing the like exploit of Shamgar and observing that a well-armed champion might cut down whole companies of ordinary fighting-men.
themes: These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the Lord concerning Israel.

20.pericope_label: And Abishai the brother of Joab, he was chief of the three: for lifting up his spear against three hundred, he slew them, and had a name among the three. Of the three, he was more honourable than the two; for he was their captain: howbeit he attained not to the first three. Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done many acts; he slew two lionlike men of Moab: also he went down and slew a lion in a pit in a snowy day. And he slew an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits high; and in the Egyptian’s hand was a spear like a weaver’s beam; and he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and slew him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and had the name among the three mighties. Behold, he was honourable among the thirty, but attained not to the first three: and David set him over his guard.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads verse 21 as an exegetical alteration of Samuel meaning that Abishai was the most honoured of the second triad, and insists that Benaiah's differing word for staff shows the resemblance to the Goliath story is factual and not literary; Delitzsch renders the same phrase as doubly honoured and defends the received text against Bertheau.

Clarke twice prints the Targum, which makes Benaiah a man fearing sin who read the law on a short winter's day and turns David's guard into his disciples; Wesley reduces the crux of verse 21 to four words.

debates: How to construe verse 21: Ellicott takes "in the two" as evidence of a second triad, Delitzsch takes it as doubly honoured, and each rejects a different proposed emendation.
Whether "over his guard" means the Cherethites and Pelethites, as Ellicott holds, or a body of disciples, as the Targum Clarke prints would have it.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the exploit credited to Abishai is described in the very words used of Jashobeam.

26.pericope_label: Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Beth–lehem, Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Abi–ezer the Antothite, Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite, Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah, that pertained to the children of Benjamin, Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai, Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Berothite, the armourbearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite, Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the list with the corps called the Thirty, notes that the men down to verse 41 are paired and mostly of Judah and Benjamin while the sixteen appended names are transjordanic, and repairs a long series of corrupted names; Delitzsch reports Bertheau and Reland on the last two forms without adjudicating.
Wesley explains the sixteen additional names as commanders of great valour who were not of the thirty, and reads the thirty of verse 42 as captains under Adina as their colonel.

Henry raises the presence of an Ammonite and a Moabite against the law of Deuteronomy 23:3, and concludes that the exception was an early indication that the Son of David would have worthies among the Gentiles.

debates: Why sixteen names stand beyond Samuel's closing total of thirty and seven: Ellicott suspects a later revision of the catalogue, Wesley a second rank of commanders.
Whether the thirty of verse 42 are men under Adina or captains under him.
Whether the aliens in the list are merely a fact about David's service, as Ellicott takes them, or a deliberate dispensation from the law, as Henry argues.
outliers: Ellicott wonders whether Elhanan son of Dodo is a third alias of the slayer of Goliath, on the ground that Dodo is very much like David.
